section_title: STW Title & Classification: Respiratory Distress in Neonates
text:
Standard Treatment Workﬂow (STW)
RESPIRATORY DISTRESS IN NEONATES
ICD 11- KB23
Department of Health Research
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare,
Government of India

section_title: Diagnostic Criteria: Respiratory Distress in Neonates
text:
RESPIRATORY DISTRESS
Presence of ANY ONE:
• RR >60/min
• Chest retractions
• Nasal ﬂaring
• Grunting

section_title: Immediate Actions for Neonatal Respiratory Distress
text:
IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
• Assess and stabilize TABC (temperature, airway, breathing, circulation)
• Admit to SNCU/NICU
◦Provide thermal care
◦Attach pulse oximeter
◦Monitor HR, RR, SpO₂ and CRT; grade severity using Silverman-Andersen score (SAS)
• Feed enterally if stable 
◦Direct breastfeed if mild distress; gastric-tube feeds if moderate distress, or on CPAP
• IV ﬂuids if severe distress, recurrent apnea, poor perfusion, or abdominal signs

section_title: Algorithm: Respiratory Distress Gestational Age & SAS Assessment
text:
ALGORITHM
RESPIRATORY DISTRESS Assess gestation (GA) + SAS
If GA is uncertain, BW ≤1800 g may be used as an operational surrogate

section_title: Initial Respiratory Support for GA ≤34 Weeks (CPAP & Caffeine Citrate)
text:
GA ≤34 weeks
Any respiratory distress
START CPAP
CPAP 5–6 cm H₂O; use blended O₂ and titrate FiO₂ to maintain SpO₂ 91–95%
Start caffeine citrate in neonates <34 weeks who require respiratory support

section_title: Initial Support for GA >34 Weeks with Moderate-to-Severe Distress (SAS ≥4)
text:
GA >34 weeks
Moderate-severe RD  (SAS ≥4)
START CPAP
CPAP 5–6 cm H₂O; use blended O₂ and titrate FiO₂ to maintain SpO₂ 91–95%

section_title: Initial Support for GA >34 Weeks with Mild Distress (SAS ≤3)
text:
GA >34 weeks
Mild RD (SAS ≤3)
NASAL-PRONG OXYGEN 0.5–1 L/min
Titrate to SpO₂ 91–95%

section_title: Reassessment Protocol & Sepsis Consideration
text:
REASSESS FREQUENTLY: clinical status, SAS, SpO₂, FiO₂ requirement
Consider sepsis if perinatal risk factors, systemic illness, worsening distress or rising FiO₂ (see STW: Sepsis in Neonates)

section_title: Outcome Improving: CPAP and Oxygen Weaning Protocol
text:
IMPROVING
• Decreasing SAS 
• SpO₂ 91–95% on stable/reducing support
• Comfortable breathing
Wean FiO₂ ﬁrst to 0.21, then 
reduce CPAP in 1 cm H₂O steps to
4–5 cm H₂O and stop when 
stable; continue SpO₂ monitoring
for 24 h after stopping

section_title: Surfactant Therapy Indication & Thresholds
text:
SURFACTANT
<34 weeks on CPAP 
needing PEEP >6 cm H₂O
AND FiO₂ >0.30 to keep
SpO₂ between 91-95%

section_title: Outcome Not Improving: Steps to Optimize CPAP
text:
NOT IMPROVING/WORSENING
• Persisting/increasing SAS
• SpO₂ <91% or rising oxygen need
• Recurrent apnea/bradycardia
• Fatigue, shock or deterioration
OPTIMIZE CPAP
• Increase PEEP stepwise up to 7–8 cm H₂O
• Titrate FiO₂ to target SpO₂ 91–95%
• Look for/treat underlying cause
• Consider surfactant if criteria met

section_title: CPAP Failure Criteria & Urgent Referral Indication
text:
CPAP FAILURE 
Persistent hypoxemia/high FiO₂ requirement, 
recurrent apnea, shock or fatigue →  Refer urgently

section_title: Clinical DOs for Neonatal Respiratory Distress
text:
DOs
• Assess severity using SAS and monitor SpO₂ continuously
• Maintain SpO₂ 91%-95%.
• Start CPAP within 30 minutes
• Administer surfactant within 2 hours

section_title: Clinical DON'Ts for Neonatal Respiratory Distress
text:
DON’Ts
• DO NOT give unmonitored supplemental oxygen.
• DO NOT perform routine CBC, CRP, Chest X-ray or blood gas in 
uncomplicated mild RD
• DO NOT give IV ﬂuids, antibiotics, or blood products routinely
• DO NOT delay mechanical ventilation or referral in case of CPAP 
failure

section_title: Key Performance Indicators (KPIs): Respiratory Distress Management
text:
KEY PERFORMANCE INDICATORS (KPIs)
Timely CPAP initiation (%)  =  Neonates ≤34 weeks with RD started on CPAP within 30 min of diagnosis or admission x 100
(Target >90%)  
 
         Neonates ≤34  weeks diagnosed with RD
SpO₂ target compliance (%) =  Neonates receiving supplemental oxygen or CPAP with continuous pulse oximetry and SpO2 in target range × 100
(Target >90%)  
 
           Neonates receiving supplemental oxygen or CPAP

section_title: Silverman-Andersen Score (SAS) Methodology & Interpretation
text:
SILVERMAN ANDERSEN SCORE (SAS)
ASSESS SAS • PROVIDE APPROPRIATE RESPIRATORY SUPPORT • TARGET SPO2 91–95% • ESCALATE
SUPPORT PROMPTLY IF NOT IMPROVING
Figure: The Silverman score for assessing the magnitude of respiratory
distress. (From Avery, M.E., and Fletcher, B.D.: The Lung and Its 
Disorders in the Newborn. Philadelphia, W.B. Saunders Company, 
1974) (Courtesy of W.A. Silverman)

scoring

section_title: STW Title & Definition: Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP)
text:
Standard Treatment Workﬂow (STW)
RETINOPATHY OF PREMATURITY (ROP)
ICD-11-9B71.3
Department of Health Research
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare,
Government of India
ROP is a potentially blinding retinal vascular disorder of preterm infants. Severe disease may cause retinal 
detachment and irreversible vision loss. Optimal quality neonatal care, timely screening and prompt 
treatment can prevent most ROP-related blindness.

section_title: Whom to Screen: ROP Screening Eligibility Criteria
text:
WHOM TO SCREEN
Screen if any ONE of the following is present:
• Gestation <34 weeks
• Birth weight <2000 g
• Gestation 34-36 weeks with speciﬁed risk 
factors* or an unstable clinical course
*Signiﬁcant cardiorespiratory support, 
prolonged/poorly controlled oxygen therapy, 
signiﬁcant anemia, blood transfusion, sepsis,
poor postnatal weight gain

section_title: When to Screen: Timing of First Screening & Follow-up Intervals
text:
WHEN TO SCREEN
First screen:
• By 4 weeks postnatal age
• By 2-3 weeks postnatal age, if GA <28 
weeks or BW <1200 g
• If already overdue, screen ASAP
• If follow-up uncertain, screen before 
discharge even if not due
Repeat screen:
• As per advice by ROP-trained 
ophthalmologist according to retinal 
ﬁndings, usually every 1-3 weeks
• Posterior or progressive disease/suspected 
A-ROP may require review within 1 week or 
sooner

section_title: How to Arrange Screening: SNCU/NICU & Referral Protocols
text:
HOW TO ARRANGE SCREENING
• Preferred: On-site screening in SNCU/ 
NICU by an ROP-trained 
ophthalmologist/tele-screening team 
with appropriate monitoring
• If unavailable: Arrange scheduled 
specialist visits, or safe referral to the 
nearest designated ROP screening 
centre

section_title: Prepare to Screen: Feeding, Pupillary Dilation & Swaddling
text:
PREPARE TO SCREEN
• Withhold feeds - 1 hour before screening
• Dilate pupils: phenylephrine 2.5% +  
tropicamide 0.5-0.8% eye drops (2-3 
times at 10 min interval)                                                            
• Swaddle, proparacaine eye drops, EBM/ 
oral 25% dextrose for analgesia 
• Maintain temperature and monitor SpO2

section_title: How to Screen: Clinical Examination Technique
text:
HOW TO SCREEN
• Strict hand hygiene and asepsis
• Examine both eyes by indirect 
ophthalmoscopy (20D/28D lens); use 
speculum/scleral indentation as required
• Wide-ﬁeld retinal imaging/tele- 
screening may be used where available
• Monitor for apnea, bradycardia,  
desaturation and feed intolerance
• Document ROP ﬁndings and the 
date/place of the next examination

section_title: Treatment Indications: ICROP Criteria & Treatment Urgency
text:
TREATMENT INDICATIONS
• Zone I: Any stage with plus disease, or 
stage 3 without plus
• Zone II: Stage 2-3 with plus disease
• Aggressive ROP (A-ROP): Urgent 
treatment
• Reactivation/signiﬁcant PAR after 
anti-VEGF; stage 2–3; stage 4–5 
• Advanced ROP (Stage 4-5): Requires 
referral for surgery
Treatment-requiring ROP should be treated
urgently, preferably within 48-72 hours of
the decision to treat

section_title: Treatment Options: Laser Photocoagulation & Anti-VEGF
text:
TREATMENT OPTIONS
• Laser photocoagulation and/or 
intravitreal anti-VEGF injection, as 
decided by the ROP specialist based on 
zone and disease characteristics.
• Vitreo-retinal surgery for advanced ROP

section_title: When to Stop Screening: Criteria for Termination of Screening
text:
WHEN TO STOP SCREENING
PREVENTION
• Stop only when advised by ROP-trained 
ophthalmologist (retina fully vascularised, 
or ROP fully regressed)
• After anti-VEGF treatment, prolonged 
follow-up at least until 65 weeks PMA is 
required because of the risk of late 
reactivation and persistent avascular retina 
(PAR)

section_title: Prevention of ROP: Antenatal Steroids & Safe Oxygenation
text:
• Antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung 
maturation
• Safe oxygen therapy
◦Use air-oxygen blenders and 
continuous pulse oximetry
◦Target SpO2 : 91-95%
• Prevent and promptly treat sepsis
• Ensure mother’s own milk, optimal 
nutrition and adequate postnatal growth 
• Avoid unnecessary blood transfusions

section_title: Clinical DOs for Retinopathy of Prematurity
text:
DOs
DON’Ts
• Ensure timely ROP screening and follow-up 
• Document the date and place of next screening in discharge card
• Counsel the family regarding need for follow-up and risk of vision 
loss if screening is delayed

section_title: Clinical DON'Ts for Retinopathy of Prematurity
text:
• DO NOT discharge/transfer an at-risk neonate without a 
documented ROP follow-up plan
• DO NOT delay referral/treatment when indicated
• DO NOT stop ROP follow-up without advice of ROP-trained 
ophthalmologist

section_title: Key Performance Indicators (KPIs): ROP Screening Coverage & Timeliness
text:
KEY PERFORMANCE INDICATORS (KPIs)
ROP screening coverage (%) = Eligible infants who received at least one ROP eye examination x 100
Total eligible infants for ROP screening
Timely ﬁrst ROP screening (%) = Eligible infants screened within the recommended ﬁrst-screen window x 100
Eligible infants due for ﬁrst screening
    All SNCUs/NICUs should periodically assess the KPIs and undertake quality improvement measures to achieve 95-100% compliance

section_title: Key Clinical Imperative: No Infant Leaves Without Screening Plan
text:
TIMELY ROP SCREENING SAVES SIGHT — NO ELIGIBLE INFANT SHOULD LEAVE THE SNCU/NICU
WITHOUT SCREENING OR A DOCUMENTED FOLLOW-UP PLAN

Which signs need immediate treatment?

segments.text: Shock (cold peripheries, mottled/grey skin, CRT >3 s, weak pulses, low BP)

text:
EMERGENCY
Significant hypothermia (<35.5°C)
Apnea or gasping
Respiratory distress (retractions, grunt)
Central cyanosis or SpO₂ <91%
Shock (cold peripheries, mottled/grey skin, CRT >3 s,
weak pulses, low BP)
Convulsions/coma
Severe dehydration
Persistent tachycardia >200/min

title: Priority Signs

text:
PRIORITY

title: Non-urgent Signs

text:
NON-URGENT
Mild jaundice
Transitional stools
Minor birth trauma
Minor malformations
Superficial infections
Breastfeeding difficulty
Regurgitation

title: Treat Immediately: Emergency Actions
example_questions: What should be done immediately for emergency signs?
What respiratory support does the triage STW recommend?
What are the immediate emergency actions?

segments.text: Respiratory support: Nasal prong O₂ if SpO₂ <91% (titrate to 91–95%); nasal CPAP if respiratory distress; intubate if gasping or poor effort.
Check blood glucose; send CBC and electrolytes
If sepsis is likely, draw blood culture and give the first antibiotic dose without delay
Start IV fluids as per weight and postnatal age

text:
TREAT IMMEDIATELY
Maintain TABC
Respiratory support: Nasal prong O₂ if SpO₂ <91%
(titrate to 91–95%); nasal CPAP if respiratory distress;
intubate if gasping or poor effort.
Check blood glucose; send CBC and electrolytes
If sepsis is likely, draw blood culture and give the first
antibiotic dose without delay
Start IV fluids as per weight and postnatal age
Manage shock, dehydration and seizures

title: Assess Promptly and Act Rapidly

segments.text: Check blood glucose and act accordingly
Start IV fluids (if abdominal distension/GI malformation) or gavage feeds
Assess the risk factors for sepsis

text:

Check blood glucose and act accordingly

title: Specific Management: Shock
example_questions: How does the triage STW manage shock?
What IV fluid dose is listed for shock?

segments.text: IV NS 10 mL/kg if volume expansion is indicated: preterm over 30–60 min; term over 15–20 min.

text:
SHOCK
IV NS 10 mL/kg if volume expansion is indicated: preterm over 30–60 min; term over 15–20 min.
Consider inotropes early.

title: Specific Management: Severe Dehydration
example_questions: How is severe dehydration managed in the triage STW?
What is the fluid plan for diarrhoeal severe dehydration?

segments.text: (Diarrhoea plus any two of lethargy, very slow skin pinch and sunken eyes)
Diarrhoeal severe dehydration: IV RL/NS 30 mL/kg in 1 h, then 70 mL/kg over 5 h (WHO Plan C).
If IV not possible: ORS 20 mL/kg/h for 6 h. Assess 1–2 hourly and titrate fluids.
Hypernatremic dehydration related to poor feeding/hot environment: manage as per the standard neonatal protocol.

text:
SEVERE DEHYDRATION
(Diarrhoea plus any two of lethargy,
very slow skin pinch and sunken eyes)
Diarrhoeal severe dehydration: IV RL/NS 30 mL/kg in 1 h, then 70 mL/kg over 5 h (WHO Plan C).
If IV not possible: ORS 20 mL/kg/h for 6 h. Assess 1–2 hourly and titrate fluids.
Hypernatremic dehydration related to poor feeding/hot environment: manage as per the standard
neonatal protocol.

title: Specific Management: Seizures
example_questions: What seizure treatment is listed in the triage STW?
What is the phenobarbitone dose in this workflow?

segments.text: Inj. phenobarbitone 20 mg/kg IV over 15 min. If seizures persist after 15 min, give a further 10 mg/kg IV over 10 min.
If uncontrolled, consider levetiracetam as second-line treatment.
Correct glucose and calcium if abnormal, concurrently.

text:
SEIZURES
(Refer to STW on neonatal seizures)
Inj. phenobarbitone 20 mg/kg IV over 15 min. If seizures persist after 15 min, give a further 10 mg/kg IV
over 10 min.
If uncontrolled, consider levetiracetam as second-line treatment.
Correct glucose and calcium if abnormal, concurrently.

title: Specific Management: Surgical Conditions
example_questions: What does the triage STW say for surgical conditions?
What should be done for suspected TEF or oesophageal atresia?
What does the STW say about CDH ventilation?

segments.text: Cover exposed skin defects with warm saline sterile gauze; maintain hydration.
CDH: Avoid CPAP/bag-mask ventilation. Intubate if necessary; decompress stomach with an OG/NG tube.
Suspected TEF/oesophageal atresia: Nil by mouth, IV fluids, head-up position; upper-pouch suction.
Arrange urgent referral to a surgical centre.

text:

Suspected TEF/oesophageal atresia: Nil by mouth, IV fluids, head-up position; upper-pouch suction.

title: Specific Management: Persistent Heart Rate >200/min
example_questions: What should be done for persistent heart rate over 200 per minute?

segments.text: Check and correct hyperthermia; refer for further management.

text:
PERSISTENT HR
>200/MIN
Check ECG for arrhythmia.
Check and correct hyperthermia; refer for further management.

title: Specific Management: Hypothermia
example_questions: How is hypothermia managed in the triage STW?
What should be done at a temperature below 35.5 degrees?

segments.text: (Refer to STW on thermal care of newborn)
Temperature <35.5°C: nurse under a radiant warmer in servo mode.
Temperature 35.5–36.4°C and baby is well: warm environment, skin-to-skin contact; recheck in 30 min.
If unwell or temperature fails to improve, nurse under a warmer.

text:

(Refer to STW on thermal care of
newborn)

Temperature 35.5–36.4°C and baby is well: warm environment, skin-to-skin contact; recheck in 30 min.

title: Specific Management: Hypoglycemia
example_questions: What does the triage STW recommend for neonatal hypoglycemia?
What glucose level and treatment are listed for symptomatic babies?

segments.text: Blood glucose <45 mg/dL and asymptomatic: supervised breastfeeding or EBM.
Blood glucose <20 mg/dL OR symptomatic: 2 mL/kg 10% dextrose IV, followed by infusion at 6 mg/kg/min.

title: Triage DOs
example_questions: What are the DOs in the neonatal triage STW?
What should be done for every neonate on arrival?

segments.text: Screen every neonate immediately on arrival for emergency and priority signs.
Maintain TABC, assess SpO₂ and blood glucose, and start indicated treatment promptly. Reassess after each intervention.
Administer the first dose of antibiotic within 1 hour if there is a high likelihood of sepsis.

title: Triage DON'Ts
example_questions: What are the DON'Ts in the neonatal triage STW?
Should emergency treatment wait for investigations?

segments.text: Do NOT delay emergency treatment for investigations or documentation.
Obtain blood culture before the first dose of antibiotics, but do not delay treatment.
Do NOT discharge a neonate with persistent emergency or priority signs; arrange admission or appropriate referral.

title: Kangaroo Mother Care: Definition
example_questions: What is Kangaroo Mother Care?
How does the KMC STW define kangaroo mother care?

segments.text: Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) is early, continuous and prolonged skin-to-skin contact between a preterm or low birth weight newborn and the mother (or an alternate caregiver), combined with exclusive breastmilk feeding, early discharge when appropriate, and structured follow-up.

text:
Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) is early, continuous and prolonged skin-to-skin contact between a preterm or low birth weight newborn and the
mother (or an alternate caregiver), combined with exclusive breastmilk feeding, early discharge when appropriate, and structured follow-up.
